title: Nahum
summary: Nahum is a biblical book focused on Nineveh, judgment, divine justice, refuge, and the fall of oppressive empire.
historical_context: Nahum announces judgment against Nineveh and portrays the Lord as refuge and just judge.
ancient_near_east_context: Nahum belongs to the ancient Mediterranean and Near Eastern world reflected in its setting, institutions, and canonical placement.
hebraic_worldview: Nahum should be read with attention to covenant memory, communal identity, worship, wisdom, and accountability before the Lord.
second_temple_context: Second Temple readers received Nahum as part of Israel's Scriptures and read it within questions of identity, worship, exile, and hope.
canonical_context: Within Minor Prophets, book 7 of 12, Nahum contributes to the Bible's unfolding witness by connecting Nineveh, judgment, divine justice, refuge, and the fall of oppressive empire to the larger storyline.
later_christian_reception: Christian interpretation has read Nahum as part of the canonical witness to faithfulness, judgment, mercy, and hope in Christ-centered Scripture reading.
literary_context: Nahum uses prophecy, poetry within Minor Prophets, book 7 of 12 to develop its themes through the book's structure and key passages.
covenantal_significance: Nahum helps readers trace covenant faithfulness, failure, mercy, and hope within its canonical setting.
authorship_positions: Traditional prophetic attribution to the named prophet
Many scholars recognize collection and editorial shaping
date_ranges: 8th-5th centuries BCE, depending on the prophet
Final forms often reflect later collection and editing
original_audience: Israel and Judah under covenant accountability before and after exile
historical_setting: Assyrian, Babylonian, and post-exilic settings across the prophetic corpus
canonical_role: Nahum anchors Nineveh, judgment, divine justice, refuge, and the fall of oppressive empire within Minor Prophets, book 7 of 12 and connects the book to related people, places, events, and themes.
interpretive_disputes: How to read prophetic poetry, irony, and symbolic action

related_objects.notes: Nineveh is the target of the oracle.
Assyria gives the oracle its imperial setting.
Judgment against oppression dominates the book.
The book emphasizes the Lord's just response to violence.
Nahum contributes to the prophetic judgment horizon.
